*Purpose*: Creating effective data visualizations is an *iterative* process; very rarely will the first graph you make be the most effective. The most effective thing you can do to be successful in this iterative process is to *try multiple graphs* of the same data.

Furthermore, judging the effectiveness of a visual is completely dependent on *the question you are trying to answer*. A visual that is totally ineffective for one question may be perfect for answering a different question.

In this challenge, you will practice *iterating* on data visualization, and will anchor the *assessment* of your visuals using two different questions.

*Note*: Please complete your initial visual design **alone**. Work on both of your graphs alone, and save a version to your repo *before* coming together with your team. This way you can all bring a diversity of ideas to the table!

# Grading Rubric

<!-- -------------------------------------------------- -->

Unlike exercises, **challenges will be graded**. The following rubrics define how you will be graded, both on an individual and team basis.

## Individual

<!-- ------------------------- -->

| Category | Needs Improvement | Satisfactory |
|----|----|----|
| Effort | Some task **q**'s left unattempted | All task **q**'s attempted |
| Observed | Did not document observations, or observations incorrect | Documented correct observations based on analysis |
| Supported | Some observations not clearly supported by analysis | All observations clearly supported by analysis (table, graph, etc.) |
| Assessed | Observations include claims not supported by the data, or reflect a level of certainty not warranted by the data | Observations are appropriately qualified by the quality & relevance of the data and (in)conclusiveness of the support |
| Specified | Uses the phrase "more data are necessary" without clarification | Any statement that "more data are necessary" specifies which *specific* data are needed to answer what *specific* question |
| Code Styled | Violations of the [style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/) hinder readability | Code sufficiently close to the [style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/) |

## Submission

Make sure to commit both the challenge report (`report.md` file) and supporting files (`report_files/` folder) when you are done! Then submit a link to Canvas. **Your Challenge submission is not complete without all files uploaded to GitHub.**

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggrepel)
```

*Background*: The data[1] we study in this challenge report the [*minimum inhibitory concentration*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_inhibitory_concentration) (MIC) of three drugs for different bacteria. The smaller the MIC for a given drug and bacteria pair, the more practical the drug is for treating that particular bacteria. An MIC value of *at most* 0.1 is considered necessary for treating human patients.

These data report MIC values for three antibiotics---penicillin, streptomycin, and neomycin---on 16 bacteria. Bacteria are categorized into a genus based on a number of features, including their resistance to antibiotics.

```{r load}
## NOTE: If you extracted all challenges to the same location,
## you shouldn't have to change this filename
filename <- "./data/antibiotics.csv"

## Load the data
df_antibiotics <- read_csv(filename)
df_antibiotics %>% knitr::kable()
```

# Visualization

<!-- -------------------------------------------------- -->

### **q1** Prototype 5 visuals

To start, construct **5 qualitatively different visualizations of the data** `df_antibiotics`. These **cannot** be simple variations on the same graph; for instance, if two of your visuals could be made identical by calling `coord_flip()`, then these are *not* qualitatively different.

For all five of the visuals, you must show information on *all 16 bacteria*. For the first two visuals, you must *show all variables*.

*Hint 1*: Try working quickly on this part; come up with a bunch of ideas, and don't fixate on any one idea for too long. You will have a chance to refine later in this challenge.

*Hint 2*: The data `df_antibiotics` are in a *wide* format; it may be helpful to `pivot_longer()` the data to make certain visuals easier to construct.

#### Visual 1 (All variables)

In this visual you must show *all three* effectiveness values for *all 16 bacteria*. This means **it must be possible to identify each of the 16 bacteria by name.** You must also show whether or not each bacterium is Gram positive or negative.

```{r q1.1}
df_long <-
  df_antibiotics |>
  mutate(bacteria = fct_reorder(bacteria, penicillin)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(penicillin, streptomycin, neomycin),
    names_to = "antibiotic",
    values_to = "mic"
  ) |>
  mutate(antibiotic = fct_relevel(antibiotic, "penicillin", "streptomycin"))

df_long |>
  ggplot(aes(mic, bacteria, color = antibiotic)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_grid(gram ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "MIC (log scale), dashed line is the 0.1 treatment cutoff",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Antibiotic"
  )
```

#### Visual 2 (All variables)

In this visual you must show *all three* effectiveness values for *all 16 bacteria*. This means **it must be possible to identify each of the 16 bacteria by name.** You must also show whether or not each bacterium is Gram positive or negative.

Note that your visual must be *qualitatively different* from *all* of your other visuals.

```{r q1.2}
df_long |>
  ggplot(aes(antibiotic, mic, group = bacteria, color = gram)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = . %>% filter(antibiotic == "neomycin"),
    mapping = aes(label = bacteria),
    size = 3,
    direction = "y",
    nudge_x = 0.3,
    hjust = 0,
    segment.alpha = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  expand_limits(x = 5) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "MIC (log scale)",
    color = "Gram stain"
  )
```

#### Visual 3 (Some variables)

In this visual you may show a *subset* of the variables (`penicillin`, `streptomycin`, `neomycin`, `gram`), but you must still show *all 16 bacteria*.

Note that your visual must be *qualitatively different* from *all* of your other visuals.

```{r q1.3}
df_antibiotics |>
  ggplot(aes(penicillin, streptomycin, color = gram)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = bacteria), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Penicillin MIC (log scale)",
    y = "Streptomycin MIC (log scale)",
    color = "Gram stain"
  )
```

#### Visual 4 (Some variables)

In this visual you may show a *subset* of the variables (`penicillin`, `streptomycin`, `neomycin`, `gram`), but you must still show *all 16 bacteria*.

Note that your visual must be *qualitatively different* from *all* of your other visuals.

```{r q1.4}
df_long |>
  ggplot(aes(gram, mic)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ antibiotic) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Gram stain",
    y = "MIC (log scale)"
  )
```

#### Visual 5 (Some variables)

In this visual you may show a *subset* of the variables (`penicillin`, `streptomycin`, `neomycin`, `gram`), but you must still show *all 16 bacteria*.

Note that your visual must be *qualitatively different* from *all* of your other visuals.

```{r q1.5}
df_antibiotics |>
  mutate(bacteria = fct_reorder(bacteria, penicillin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(penicillin, bacteria, fill = gram)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    x = "Penicillin MIC (log scale)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Gram stain"
  )
```

### **q2** Assess your visuals

There are **two questions** below; use your five visuals to help answer both Guiding Questions. Note that you must also identify which of your five visuals were most helpful in answering the questions.

*Hint 1*: It's possible that *none* of your visuals is effective in answering the questions below. You may need to revise one or more of your visuals to answer the questions below!

*Hint 2*: It's **highly unlikely** that the same visual is the most effective at helping answer both guiding questions. **Use this as an opportunity to think about why this is.**

#### Guiding Question 1

> How do the three antibiotics vary in their effectiveness against bacteria of different genera and Gram stain?

*Observations*

- What is your response to the question above?
  - First thing I had to deal with is that the MIC numbers span about 6 orders of magnitude, 0.001 up to 870. On a linear axis everything under 1 collapses into the baseline, so I put every plot on a log scale. All the comparisons below are ratios, not differences.
  - Penicillin splits on Gram stain. All 9 gram negative bacteria are above the 0.1 cutoff, most of them way above, up around 800 to 870. Almost all the gram positive ones are far below it, down around 0.001 to 0.03. The two medians are 100 and 0.005, so about 4 orders of magnitude apart. In visual 4 the two penicillin boxes don't overlap at all.
  - Treating 0.1 as the spec, penicillin basically acts like a pass/fail test on Gram stain. If I had to pick one number to separate the two groups it'd be a penicillin MIC around 0.1, and that misclassifies exactly one bacterium.
  - That one is Streptococcus fecalis. Gram positive but its penicillin MIC is 1, over the cutoff. It's also the only thing bridging the gap, the next highest gram positive is 0.03 and the lowest gram negative is 1. Take fecalis out and the two groups don't touch at all.
  - Streptomycin and neomycin don't split by Gram stain at all. In visual 4 their boxes overlap almost completely and both medians sit right around the cutoff. For those two the Gram stain tells you basically nothing.
  - Counting how many bacteria each drug gets under 0.1: neomycin 9 out of 16, penicillin 6, streptomycin 4. But penicillin's 6 are all gram positive while neomycin's 9 are spread across both types.
  - On genus, the two Staphylococcus species sit at almost the same spot on all three drugs and all three clear the cutoff for them. The three Streptococcus don't agree with each other at all. Two of them are way under the cutoff on penicillin and 100x over it on the other two, and fecalis is middling on everything.
  - There are only 16 bacteria here and most genera show up once. With one bacterium per genus I can't separate a genus effect from just that one species being weird. I'd want several species per genus, and this data only has that for Streptococcus, Staphylococcus and Salmonella.
- Which of your visuals above (1 through 5) is **most effective** at helping to answer this question?
  - Visual 1.
- Why?
  - The question asks about two things, Gram stain and genus, and visual 1 is the only one that does both. Faceting by gram separates the two groups so you can see the penicillin split, and the names are still on the y axis so I can look at genus patterns like the two Staphylococcus rows.
  - Visual 4 shows the Gram stain part better, that gap between the penicillin boxes is huge. But it has no names so it says nothing about genus. If the question was only about Gram stain I'd pick 4.
  - Visuals 3 and 5 only have one or two of the drugs so they can't compare all three.

#### Guiding Question 2

In 1974 *Diplococcus pneumoniae* was renamed *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, and in 1984 *Streptococcus fecalis* was renamed *Enterococcus fecalis* [2].

> Why was *Diplococcus pneumoniae* was renamed *Streptococcus pneumoniae*?

*Observations*

- What is your response to the question above?
  - Because its MIC numbers look almost exactly like the other Streptococcus. Diplococcus pneumonia is 0.005 penicillin, 11 streptomycin, 10 neomycin. Streptococcus hemolyticus is 0.001, 14, 10. Streptococcus viridans is 0.005, 10, 40. All three have the same shape, tiny penicillin number and big numbers for the other two drugs.
  - In visual 2 the Diplococcus line and the Streptococcus hemolyticus line basically sit on top of each other the whole way across, and viridans runs parallel just above them. Nothing else on that plot does that. The background says genus is decided partly on resistance to antibiotics, so if a bacterium reacts to all three drugs the same way the Streptococcus do, that's an argument it belongs in that group.
  - Streptococcus fecalis doesn't match. It's 1, 1, 0.1, a flat line in visual 2 while the other three shoot upward. So it was already the odd one out in its own genus before anyone renamed it, and the prompt says it became Enterococcus later.
  - This is three numbers on one bacterium though. With 16 rows and 3 columns, two things landing close on all three could just be luck, and I don't have a way to check that from this data. Real reclassification would use way more than antibiotic resistance and I don't know what else went into it. The data fits the rename, that's all I can say from here.
- Which of your visuals above (1 through 5) is **most effective** at helping to answer this question?
  - Visual 2.
- Why?
  - I need to compare whole profiles here, not single numbers. In visual 2 each bacterium is a line across the three drugs, so two that act the same end up as two lines sitting on top of each other. You just see it.
  - Visual 1 has the same information. The Diplococcus row even sits right between viridans and hemolyticus because I sorted by penicillin. But I have to check three dot positions across three rows to catch it, which is slower and easy to miss.
  - Visual 3 is a decent runner up, those three cluster in the top left away from everything else. It drops neomycin though.
  - Different visual than question 1, which I didn't expect going in. I think it's because question 1 was comparing groups and question 2 was matching one thing against a group, and those need different plots.
